lists.text:
1. Launch a citywide curbside compost collection program that accepts all food scraps, including meat and dairy.
2. Require grocery stores above a certain size to donate edible unsold food to registered charities.
3. Create a city-run online map showing every food bank, pantry, and community fridge location in real time.
4. Fund a network of public community fridges in high-traffic neighborhoods where residents can leave and take surplus food.
5. Offer property tax credits to restaurants that document consistent food donations.
6. Standardize "best by" and "use by" date labeling guidance for local producers to reduce consumer confusion.
7. Run a public awareness campaign explaining that "best by" dates indicate quality, not safety.
8. Partner with schools to implement "offer versus serve" lunch policies so students take only what they will eat.
9. Install share tables in school cafeterias where students can leave unopened items for others.
10. Introduce pay-as-you-throw trash fees that charge households based on the volume of waste they produce.
11. Ban food waste from landfills for large commercial generators like hotels, hospitals, and universities.
12. Build or contract an anaerobic digester that converts food waste into biogas for city vehicles.
13. Provide free countertop compost bins to every household that signs up for organics collection.
14. Host free monthly workshops at libraries on meal planning, food storage, and cooking with leftovers.
15. Develop a city-branded app that alerts users to discounted near-expiry food at participating stores.
16. Encourage restaurants to offer smaller portion options at reduced prices.
17. Normalize take-home containers by having the city supply compostable to-go boxes to small eateries at cost.
18. Support a volunteer "food rescue" courier program that picks up surplus from businesses using bikes or cars.
19. Integrate food rescue pickups into existing city delivery or fleet routes during off-peak hours.
20. Establish a gleaning program that organizes volunteers to harvest unpicked crops from nearby farms.
21. Map and harvest fruit from public and private urban fruit trees that would otherwise drop and rot.
22. Create a "ugly produce" marketplace at farmers markets for cosmetically imperfect fruits and vegetables.
23. Offer grants to grocery stores that redesign displays to avoid overstocking perishables.
24. Fund a commercial kitchen where surplus produce is processed into soups, sauces, and frozen meals for shelters.
25. Partner with culinary schools to have students cook donated surplus food as part of their training.
26. Require caterers working on city contracts to have a documented surplus donation plan.
27. Publicize the federal Good Samaritan Food Donation Act so businesses understand their liability protections.
28. Host a free legal clinic for businesses with questions about food donation regulations.
29. Conduct an annual citywide waste audit to identify which sectors generate the most food waste.
30. Publish a public dashboard tracking the city's food waste reduction progress.
31. Set a formal city target, such as cutting food waste 50% by 2030, and report on it annually.
32. Appoint a dedicated food systems coordinator within city government.
33. Form a food waste task force of businesses, nonprofits, farmers, and residents.
34. Give restaurants free access to food-waste tracking software for one year.
35. Train food-service workers on inventory rotation using first-in, first-out practices.
36. Offer certification badges to "Zero Waste Kitchen" restaurants that meet reduction benchmarks.
37. Encourage hospitals to adopt room-service-style ordering for patients instead of preset trays.
38. Help senior centers and nursing homes adjust portion sizes based on resident feedback.
39. Distribute fridge thermometers to households, since many refrigerators run too warm and spoil food faster.
40. Provide printed guides showing where in the fridge different foods last longest.
41. Promote freezer-friendly cooking through social media recipes and short videos.
42. Run a "leftover makeover" recipe contest with prizes from local businesses.
43. Partner with local chefs to host pop-up dinners made entirely from rescued food.
44. Establish a food waste curriculum module for elementary and middle school science classes.
45. Create school garden programs that compost cafeteria scraps to grow vegetables.
46. Support backyard composting with subsidized bins and online tutorials.
47. Offer vermicomposting starter kits for apartment dwellers with limited space.
48. Place public compost drop-off sites at farmers markets, parks, and transit stations.
49. Require new multifamily buildings to include space for organics collection bins.
50. Give the resulting city compost back to residents and community gardens for free.
51. Partner with local farms to take food scraps for animal feed where regulations allow.
52. Connect breweries with farmers who can use spent grain as livestock feed.
53. Support startups that upcycle food byproducts into new products like flour from spent grain or juice pulp crackers.
54. Create a food business incubator specifically for upcycled food ventures.
55. Encourage grocers to sell bulk items so shoppers can buy exactly the quantity they need.
56. Ask grocery stores to end "buy one, get one free" deals on perishables in favor of simple discounts.
57. Promote dynamic pricing at stores that automatically discounts items as they near expiration.
58. Encourage supermarkets to turn aging produce into prepared foods at their in-store delis.
59. Support cold storage upgrades for food pantries so they can accept more perishable donations.
60. Provide refrigerated vans to nonprofits for transporting rescued perishable food.
61. Create a shared cold storage hub where small farmers and pantries can store food.
62. Offer business-to-business surplus exchange platforms so a restaurant can sell excess ingredients to another.
63. Encourage event venues to require attendees to RSVP accurately to improve catering estimates.
64. Set food waste guidelines for city-sponsored festivals, including donation and composting stations.
65. Station volunteer "waste ambassadors" at large public events to help people sort food scraps correctly.
66. Encourage universities to remove trays from dining halls, which reduces how much students take.
67. Help corporate cafeterias adopt pre-order systems to better forecast meals.
68. Support pantries in shifting to a client-choice model so people select food they will actually eat.
69. Offer culturally appropriate foods at pantries so donated items match community preferences.
70. Partner with faith communities to redistribute food from congregational events and meals.
71. Recognize top food-donating businesses with an annual mayoral award.
72. Provide sticker labels to residents for marking dates on leftovers and opened containers.
73. Run a "Eat This First" fridge bin campaign encouraging households to designate a shelf for food nearing expiration.
74. Launch a neighborhood food-sharing app or support existing ones like Olio.
75. Encourage local news outlets to run a weekly food-saving tip segment.
76. Partner with landlords to include composting and food storage guides in welcome packets for new tenants.
77. Incorporate food waste reduction into city employee wellness and sustainability trainings.
78. Model best practices by eliminating food waste in city hall cafeterias and meetings.
79. Offer small grants for neighborhood groups that start community canning or preserving clubs.
80. Lend out canning, dehydrating, and pickling equipment through the public library system.
81. Host seasonal preserving workshops when local produce is most abundant.
82. Encourage farmers markets to bundle end-of-day produce into discounted "rescue boxes."
83. Support community-supported agriculture programs that let members pick flexible share sizes.
84. Help farmers connect with processors who can use seconds and surplus crops.
85. Fund research partnerships with local universities on food waste measurement and solutions.
86. Provide technical assistance to food manufacturers to reduce waste in production lines.
87. Encourage packaging innovations like resealable and portion-sized containers for local products.
88. Work with delivery apps to allow restaurants to list surplus meals at discounted prices near closing time.
89. Support "pay what you can" community cafés that cook with rescued ingredients.
90. Establish a food waste hotline residents can call for composting and donation questions.
91. Give stores and restaurants clear signage templates encouraging customers to take leftovers home.
92. Partner with grocery delivery services to donate canceled or rejected orders.
93. Encourage hotels to donate untouched breakfast buffet items and adopt made-to-order options.
94. Coordinate with airports or transit hubs to rescue unsold food from concession vendors.
95. Require food waste reporting from large generators to improve data and accountability.
96. Offer reduced commercial waste hauling rates for businesses that separate organics.
97. Encourage sports stadiums and arenas to donate unsold concessions after games.
98. Run a household "food waste challenge" where families track and reduce their waste for a month.
99. Collaborate with nearby cities to share infrastructure like digesters or compost facilities.
100. Celebrate an annual city Food Waste Awareness Week with events, cooking demos, and volunteer opportunities.

lists.text:
1. Launch a citywide public awareness campaign explaining the difference between "best by," "sell by," and "use by" date labels.
2. Offer free compost bins to households that sign up for a home composting workshop.
3. Add curbside organic waste collection alongside regular trash and recycling pickup.
4. Create a municipal food recovery app that connects restaurants with surplus food to nearby shelters.
5. Provide tax incentives for grocery stores that donate unsold edible food.
6. Require large food-generating businesses to separate organic waste from landfill trash.
7. Establish community fridges in high-traffic neighborhoods where residents can leave and take food freely.
8. Partner with local farms to glean unharvested crops for food banks.
9. Offer restaurants grants to purchase food waste tracking scales and software.
10. Encourage school cafeterias to schedule recess before lunch so children eat more of their meals.
11. Set up "share tables" in schools where students can leave unopened items for others.
12. Host monthly "ugly produce" markets selling cosmetically imperfect fruits and vegetables at a discount.
13. Train volunteer "food waste ambassadors" to educate neighbors about meal planning and storage.
14. Distribute free refrigerator storage guides showing which produce lasts longest in which drawer.
15. Build a municipal anaerobic digester to convert food scraps into biogas and fertilizer.
16. Charge variable trash fees based on volume to motivate households to divert food waste.
17. Fund a commercial kitchen where volunteers turn donated surplus ingredients into frozen meals.
18. Require city-catered events to plan portions using attendance data and donate leftovers.
19. Partner with local breweries to send spent grain to bakeries and livestock farmers.
20. Offer cooking classes at libraries focused on using leftovers and food scraps.
21. Encourage restaurants to offer smaller portion sizes at reduced prices.
22. Promote "take-home container" programs where restaurants provide compostable boxes by default.
23. Create a recognition program certifying businesses that meet food waste reduction targets.
24. Pass a Good Samaritan ordinance reinforcing liability protections for food donors.
25. Provide refrigerated trucks to food rescue organizations to expand their pickup capacity.
26. Encourage grocery stores to adopt dynamic pricing that discounts items nearing expiration.
27. Establish a citywide food waste reduction goal with annual public progress reports.
28. Conduct waste audits at municipal buildings to identify the largest sources of food waste.
29. Support community gardens that accept neighborhood compost and return produce to residents.
30. Partner with hospitals to implement room-service-style ordering that reduces untouched meal trays.
31. Offer small business loans for startups that upcycle food byproducts into new products.
32. Encourage farmers markets to donate unsold produce at closing time.
33. Create drop-off compost sites at farmers markets and transit stations.
34. Launch a social media challenge encouraging residents to post meals made from leftovers.
35. Integrate food waste lessons into the K-12 science and health curriculum.
36. Partner with universities to research local food waste patterns and solutions.
37. Encourage dining halls at colleges to go trayless to reduce over-serving.
38. Provide free freezer bags and labels at libraries to promote freezing surplus food.
39. Organize community canning and preserving days during harvest season.
40. Support food co-ops that buy in bulk and let members purchase exact quantities.
41. Encourage grocery stores to sell loose produce instead of pre-packaged multi-packs.
42. Fund a "food waste hotline" residents can call for storage and recipe advice.
43. Require new commercial developments to include space for organics collection bins.
44. Create a donation matching service for caterers and wedding venues.
45. Partner with apartment complexes to install shared compost collection stations.
46. Pilot a food scrap collection program using cargo bikes in dense neighborhoods.
47. Offer restaurants free consultations with chefs trained in zero-waste menu design.
48. Encourage menu items that use whole animals and whole vegetables, such as stems and peels.
49. Partner with local pig farmers to safely use permitted food scraps as animal feed.
50. Support insect farming facilities that convert food waste into protein for animal feed.
51. Provide municipal employees with training on reducing waste in break rooms and events.
52. Install smart bins in public spaces that measure and report food waste levels.
53. Host an annual food waste hackathon to develop local tech solutions.
54. Create a public dashboard showing how much food the city diverts from landfills.
55. Encourage grocery stores to use better inventory forecasting software.
56. Offer discounted produce boxes of surplus items through a subscription program.
57. Partner with food trucks to sell end-of-day items at reduced prices.
58. Launch a "Love Your Leftovers" restaurant week featuring dishes made from surplus ingredients.
59. Provide multilingual food storage and composting materials for immigrant communities.
60. Encourage faith communities to organize meal-sharing programs with donated food.
61. Fund pantry staff training on safe handling and redistribution of perishable donations.
62. Ban edible food from being disposed of in landfills by large supermarkets.
63. Create a backyard chicken program allowing households to feed kitchen scraps to hens.
64. Support senior centers in sharing surplus meals with homebound residents.
65. Encourage meal kit services to donate unused ingredients to local charities.
66. Install community compost tumblers in parks maintained by volunteers.
67. Offer workplace challenges rewarding offices that cut cafeteria waste the most.
68. Provide free food waste reduction toolkits to new homeowners and renters.
69. Encourage hotels to replace large breakfast buffets with made-to-order options.
70. Partner with sports stadiums to donate unsold concessions after games.
71. Encourage bakeries to sell day-old bread at discounted prices or donate it nightly.
72. Support local juice makers in turning bruised fruit into beverages.
73. Create a city grant for neighborhood groups running food rescue programs.
74. Use municipal compost in city parks and landscaping projects to close the loop.
75. Sell finished city compost to residents at low cost to fund the program.
76. Encourage grocery stores to set aside a "rescued food" section for imperfect items.
77. Develop clear guidelines for daycare centers on safely saving and sharing leftovers.
78. Partner with delivery drivers to transport donations during off-peak hours.
79. Offer workshops for small farmers on cold storage to reduce post-harvest loss.
80. Build a shared cold storage facility for local farmers and food banks.
81. Encourage schools to serve sliced fruit instead of whole fruit to increase consumption.
82. Let students choose their own sides in school lunch lines rather than receiving set portions.
83. Track and publicize school cafeteria plate waste to motivate improvement.
84. Partner with prisons and jails to improve meal planning and divert waste to compost.
85. Encourage event planners to use RSVPs to estimate food quantities accurately.
86. Provide water-efficient garbage disposal alternatives such as countertop composters at a discount.
87. Create a citywide "zero waste" event certification for festivals.
88. Support mobile food pantries that distribute perishable rescued food in underserved areas.
89. Encourage restaurants to compost kitchen prep scraps through a subsidized hauler.
90. Partner with local media to run a weekly "waste less" tip segment.
91. Offer discounted transit passes to volunteers who regularly transport rescued food.
92. Create a city procurement policy that prioritizes vendors with food waste reduction practices.
93. Encourage grocery stores to share data on wasted items to improve supply chain planning.
94. Promote meal planning apps through library and city websites.
95. Train food bank staff to quickly repurpose near-expiry donations into prepared meals.
96. Partner with culinary schools to have students cook with rescued ingredients.
97. Encourage landlords to include composting information in lease packets.
98. Pilot pay-as-you-throw organics fees to measure participation and reward reduction.
99. Partner with neighboring towns to share organics processing infrastructure and costs.
100. Appoint a city food waste coordinator to oversee and integrate all reduction efforts.

30. Encourage farmers markets to offer end-of-day discounts or donation drop-offs for unsold produce.
31. Provide community canning and food preservation classes in summer and fall.
32. Open a public tool library that lends dehydrators, pressure canners, and vacuum sealers.
33. Integrate food waste lessons into elementary and middle school science curricula.
34. Establish school garden programs that teach children the value of growing food.
35. Conduct annual waste audits of city buildings to identify where food is being thrown away.
36. Encourage grocery stores to use dynamic pricing that automatically discounts items nearing expiration.
37. Support apps like Too Good To Go by promoting them through city communications.

87. Create a public dashboard showing how much food the city has diverted from landfill.

99. Partner with faith communities to coordinate shared meals using rescued food.

lists.text:
1. Launch a citywide public awareness campaign explaining the difference between "best by," "sell by," and "use by" date labels.
2. Distribute free fridge thermometers to households so food is stored at safe temperatures and lasts longer.
3. Offer free community workshops on meal planning and smart grocery shopping.
4. Host cooking classes that teach residents how to use leftovers and food scraps creatively.
5. Provide subsidized countertop compost bins to every household that requests one.
6. Implement curbside organic waste collection alongside regular trash and recycling pickup.
7. Adopt pay-as-you-throw trash pricing so households pay less when they divert food from the landfill.
8. Partner with local grocery stores to sell "ugly" or cosmetically imperfect produce at a discount.
9. Encourage supermarkets to donate unsold but safe food to food banks through a city-coordinated pickup network.
10. Offer business tax credits for food donations made by restaurants, grocers, and caterers.
11. Publicize state and federal Good Samaritan laws that protect food donors from liability.
12. Create a city-sponsored app that connects restaurants with surplus food to nearby charities in real time.
13. Fund refrigerated vans so food rescue organizations can transport perishables safely.
14. Install public community fridges in neighborhoods where residents can share excess food.
15. Establish a municipal food waste reduction office to coordinate all programs and track progress.
16. Require large food businesses to report how much food they throw away each year.
17. Ban commercial food waste from landfills for businesses above a certain size.
18. Set a citywide goal of cutting food waste by 50 percent by a target year and publish annual progress reports.
19. Conduct a baseline waste audit to measure how much food the city discards and from which sectors.
20. Support school cafeterias in adopting "offer versus serve" policies so students take only what they will eat.
21. Set up share tables in schools where students can leave unopened food for classmates.
22. Schedule school recess before lunch, which research shows reduces plate waste.
23. Start composting programs in every public school cafeteria.
24. Integrate food waste lessons into school science and health curricula.
25. Build school gardens that teach children where food comes from and why it matters.
26. Encourage restaurants to offer smaller portion options at lower prices.
27. Promote take-home containers by giving restaurants free compostable to-go boxes.
28. Run a "doggy bag pride" campaign that normalizes taking leftovers home.
29. Offer free waste-tracking software to restaurants so they can identify and cut over-preparation.
30. Certify and publicly recognize "Zero Waste Restaurants" that meet reduction benchmarks.
31. Train commercial kitchen staff in inventory rotation methods like first-in, first-out.
32. Encourage hotels to move away from wasteful all-you-can-eat buffets or use smaller serving trays.
33. Require caterers at city-funded events to have a surplus food donation plan.
34. Partner with apps like Too Good To Go to promote discounted end-of-day food bags locally.
35. Open a city-supported nonprofit grocery that sells surplus and near-date food at low prices.
36. Support gleaning programs where volunteers harvest leftover crops from local farms.
37. Connect urban fruit tree owners with volunteers who pick and donate unwanted fruit.
38. Create a regional food hub that aggregates and distributes surplus produce from nearby farms.
39. Help local farmers access processing facilities to turn surplus crops into sauces, jams, or frozen goods.
40. Offer grants to food entrepreneurs who upcycle waste into new products like juice-pulp crackers or spent-grain bread.
41. Build a municipal composting facility that produces soil amendments for parks and residents.
42. Invest in an anaerobic digester that turns food waste into renewable energy.
43. Partner with local farms to send inedible food scraps for animal feed where safe and legal.
44. Give finished compost back to residents for free at distribution days.
45. Use city-produced compost in public parks, medians, and community gardens.
46. Establish neighborhood drop-off sites for food scraps in areas without curbside service.
47. Support community composting hubs run by local nonprofits or gardens.
48. Train "Master Composter" volunteers to educate neighbors.
49. Run a "Waste Less Week" challenge where households track and reduce their food waste.
50. Provide free "food waste diaries" or tracking tools for families who want to measure their habits.
51. Distribute fridge magnets with storage tips for common fruits and vegetables.
52. Partner with libraries to lend food preservation equipment like canners and dehydrators.
53. Host community canning and preserving workshops during harvest season.
54. Create a city website with recipes for commonly wasted foods like bread, bananas, and herbs.
55. Run social media campaigns featuring local chefs sharing leftover recipes.
56. Encourage grocery stores to sell loose produce so shoppers can buy exact quantities.
57. Discourage "buy one, get one free" promotions on perishables in favor of straightforward discounts.
58. Ask grocers to create clearly marked "reduced for quick sale" sections.
59. Encourage stores to adopt dynamic pricing that automatically discounts food nearing its date.
60. Support grocery stores in improving cold chain monitoring to prevent spoilage.
61. Incentivize retailers to install doors on open refrigerated cases to preserve food quality.
62. Partner with hospitals to reduce patient tray waste through on-demand room service menus.
63. Help senior centers and care homes adjust portion sizes to residents' actual appetites.
64. Work with corporate cafeterias to track and publicly report food waste.
65. Encourage university dining halls to go trayless, which reduces how much students take.
66. Recruit college students to run food recovery chapters on campus.
67. Require food waste reduction plans for large public events and festivals.
68. Provide sorting stations with clear signage for compost, recycling, and trash at public events.
69. Train event volunteers as "waste ambassadors" to help attendees sort correctly.
70. Arrange food truck partnerships to donate unsold meals after festivals.
71. Build city procurement policies that prioritize vendors with strong waste reduction practices.
72. Ensure city jails, shelters, and other institutions measure and reduce kitchen waste.
73. Offer zoning flexibility for small-scale composting and food processing businesses.
74. Streamline health permits for organizations that redistribute prepared food.
75. Create a city-backed microloan fund for food waste startups.
76. Host an annual food waste innovation competition with cash prizes.
77. Partner with local universities to research the city's waste patterns and test solutions.
78. Pilot smart bins that weigh and analyze food waste in commercial kitchens.
79. Support apartment buildings in adding compost collection rooms or chutes.
80. Require new multifamily developments to include organics collection infrastructure.
81. Provide landlords with toolkits for launching tenant composting programs.
82. Translate all food waste materials into the main languages spoken in the city.
83. Partner with faith communities to share surplus food from congregational meals.
84. Work with cultural organizations to highlight traditional practices for using whole ingredients.
85. Support community kitchens where volunteers cook rescued food into meals for those in need.
86. Train unemployed residents in culinary skills using rescued food through job programs.
87. Expand food bank capacity with additional cold storage space.
88. Coordinate with neighboring municipalities to share composting and food rescue resources.
89. Encourage farmers markets to sell end-of-day produce at discount or donate it.
90. Help small corner stores access refrigeration grants to sell fresh food without spoilage.
91. Promote freezer-friendly cooking and batch meal guides for busy families.
92. Ask meal kit companies operating locally to offer flexible portions and take-back packaging.
93. Encourage food delivery apps to show restaurants' surplus deals to nearby users.
94. Recognize outstanding residents and businesses with annual "Food Waste Hero" awards.
95. Publish an online map of all food donation sites, community fridges, and compost drop-offs.
96. Create a hotline businesses can call to arrange same-day food rescue pickups.
97. Include food waste reduction in the city's climate action plan with measurable targets.
98. Enforce contamination rules gently with education tags on improperly sorted organics bins.
99. Sponsor neighborhood potlucks that celebrate cooking with surplus ingredients.
100. Establish a citizen advisory council to guide and evaluate the city's food waste strategy over time.
